practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes fused deposition modelling (FDM)?
A) A laser cures liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer
B) A laser fuses metal powder layer by layer
C) A heated nozzle extrudes melted thermoplastic filament layer by layer
D) A router cuts a 3D shape from a solid block of plastic
practice_questions.marks: C) A heated nozzle extrudes melted thermoplastic filament layer by layer [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the file format used to transfer a 3D CAD model to an additive manufacturing machine.
practice_questions.type: 1 mark — Name a Material or Process
practice_questions.marks: STL (Standard Tessellation Language / stereolithography file) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why an engineer might choose additive manufacturing rather than injection moulding to produce a prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any two of:
- No tooling (mould) required, so there is no tooling cost for a one-off part
- Design can be changed quickly in CAD and re-printed, allowing rapid iteration
- Can produce complex internal geometries or undercuts that moulding cannot
- Short lead time — a prototype can be ready in hours rather than weeks
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the stages involved in producing a part using fused deposition modelling (FDM).
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any four of the following stages in a logical order:
1. Create or obtain a 3D CAD model of the part
2. Export/save the model as an STL file
3. Import the STL file into slicing software; set layer thickness and generate support structures
4. The heated nozzle melts thermoplastic filament and extrudes it onto the build platform
5. Each layer bonds to the one below as it cools; the platform lowers by one layer thickness
6. The process repeats until the part is complete; support material is removed
[4 marks — 1 mark per valid stage, must be in a logical manufacturing order]

practice_questions.text:
Holbrook Designs Ltd is a product design studio developing a new ergonomic handle for a power tool. The studio needs three prototypes to present to the client next week. The final product will be injection moulded in ABS in quantities of 50,000 units per year.

Evaluate whether additive manufacturing is a suitable choice for producing the three prototypes. In your answer, consider the advantages and limitations of additive manufacturing for this situation compared with other available methods.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Clear evaluation of both additive manufacturing and at least one alternative, with advantages and limitations linked explicitly to the details of the scenario (3 prototypes, one-week deadline, eventual high-volume injection moulding). A justified conclusion about whether additive manufacturing is suitable.

Secure (5-6 marks): Advantages and limitations both addressed with some link to the scenario. Some comparison made. Conclusion present but may be underdeveloped.

Developing (3-4 marks): Advantages or limitations covered but not both. Limited link to scenario specifics. Conclusion weak or absent.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Generic points about 3D printing with little or no reference to the scenario.

Content that may be credited:
Advantages for this scenario: no tooling cost for 3 units; STL file can be printed within the one-week deadline; design iteration is possible if changes arise; complex ergonomic geometry (curves, grip features) is achievable.
Limitations: surface finish may show layer lines (may not matter for internal client presentation but matters if the prototype is for a consumer show); material properties of FDM ABS differ from injection-moulded ABS; printing 3 units still takes several hours each.
Alternative: hand-carved foam or machined model — slower and less accurate for ergonomic geometry.
Conclusion: additive manufacturing (FDM or SLA) is well suited for this low-volume rapid prototyping task, but the studio should note that the final product will require injection moulding tooling investment before volume production.

practice_questions.text: Compare stereolithography (SLA) and metal sintering as additive manufacturing processes. In your answer, refer to the materials used, the energy source, the surface finish achieved and a typical application for each.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for developed comparative points. Up to 6 marks across the four areas:

Materials: SLA uses liquid photopolymer resin; metal sintering uses fine metal powder (e.g. stainless steel, titanium, aluminium alloy).

Energy source: SLA uses an ultraviolet laser to cure/harden the resin; metal sintering uses a high-powered infrared laser to fuse the powder particles.

Surface finish: SLA produces a very smooth surface finish with fine detail, better than FDM; metal sintering produces a slightly rough surface (powder granules) but close to the finish of machined metal.

Typical application: SLA — appearance prototypes, dental models, jewellery; metal sintering — aerospace turbine components, medical implants, lightweight structural brackets.

[6 marks — must compare, not just describe each in isolation. 1 mark per simple point, 2 marks for a developed comparative point. Max 6.]

before.content_html:
Permanent and Temporary Joining

Engineering assemblies require parts to be joined. The choice of method depends on whether the joint needs to be dismantled later, the materials being joined, the load the joint must carry and the cost of the process. Joining methods divide into two families: permanent (riveting, soldering, brazing, welding — joint cannot be undone without damaging the parts) and temporary (threaded fastenings such as bolts and screws — joint can be taken apart and reassembled). Understanding this distinction, and the temperature and filler requirements of each thermal process, is the key to answering exam questions correctly.

Riveting

Rivets are used to permanently join two or more sheets of metal. Pop (blind) rivets are used where only one side of the joint is accessible — common in aircraft skins and bodywork. Solid rivets require access to both sides: a bucking bar supports the tail while a rivet gun deforms it into a second head.

The correct sequence for riveting is one of the most-tested topics in the examination. Many students omit the marking-out stage and go straight to drilling, which means they lose marks. The full sequence is:

  1. Mark out — use a scriber and rule to mark the rivet positions on the top sheet.
  2. Centre-punch each marked position to prevent the drill wandering.
  3. Clamp the sheets together in the correct position.
  4. Drill the rivet holes through both sheets using a twist drill of the correct diameter.
  5. De-burr the holes to remove sharp edges.
  6. Insert the rivet through the aligned holes.
  7. Form the tail — use a rivet snap (or for pop rivets, the rivet gun) to peen (deform) the tail into the second head, clamping the sheets together.
Key Fact

The riveting sequence always starts with marking out. Skipping this stage — going directly from “select rivet” to “drill” — is the single most common error on joining questions and costs marks every year.

Threaded Fastenings (Temporary Joining)

Bolts, machine screws and set screws are threaded fastenings. A bolt passes through clearance holes in both parts and is secured by a nut on the reverse; a machine screw threads into a tapped hole in one part. Threaded fastenings are temporary: they can be removed with a spanner or screwdriver, which makes them essential for assemblies that need maintenance access — such as engine covers, gearbox housings and electrical panels. Locking devices (spring washers, nyloc nuts, thread-locking adhesive) prevent vibration-induced loosening.

Soft Soldering

Soft soldering uses a filler metal with a melting point below 450 °C — traditionally a tin-lead alloy, now typically lead-free tin-copper or tin-silver for health reasons. The soldering iron heats the joint; flux is applied to remove oxide films and allow the solder to flow; the filler melts and fills the gap by capillary action. The parent metal does not melt. Soft solder is used for electronic circuit-board connections and for joining copper water pipes (plumbing). The joint is weaker than the parent metal and not suitable for structural applications.

Hard soldering (also called silver soldering) uses a filler alloy containing silver, with a melting point between 450 °C and 900 °C. The process is otherwise similar to soft soldering — the parent metal is not melted — but the joint is significantly stronger and more heat-resistant. Hard soldering is used to join copper and brass components in plumbing and jewellery.

Brazing uses a brass filler rod (typically 60% copper, 40% zinc) with a melting point around 870 °C to join steel or copper parts. A blowtorch or oxy-acetylene torch heats the joint area to the correct temperature (cherry-red for steel). Flux is applied to prevent oxidation. The filler rod is touched to the hot joint and melts into the gap by capillary action — the engineer must NOT melt the filler directly in the flame. The parent metal is not melted. This is the critical distinction: brazing uses a filler rod at a temperature below the parent metal’s melting point. Welding (below) melts the parent metal itself.

A common exam error is confusing soft soldering and brazing. The temperature is the key: soft solder < 450 °C; brazing > 450 °C (typically 870 °C for brass filler). Another error is confusing brazing with welding: in brazing, the parent metal remains solid; in welding, the parent metal melts.

Welding

Welding is the only joining process listed here in which the parent metal melts. An electric arc or oxy-acetylene flame generates temperatures above the melting point of the steel (above 1,500 °C), creating a molten pool at the joint. A filler rod (or the wire electrode in MIG welding) adds material to the pool, which solidifies into a continuous fusion bond on cooling.

Common welding processes:

  • MIG (Metal Inert Gas) welding — a continuously fed wire electrode melts into the joint, shielded by an inert gas (argon or CO₂) to exclude oxygen. MIG is fast, highly controllable and widely used in vehicle body repair and fabrication workshops. BAE Systems uses MIG welding for structural steel fabrication on ships and aircraft ground equipment.
  • Arc (manual metal arc) welding — a coated electrode is clamped into a holder; the arc between electrode and workpiece melts both the electrode coating (which provides a flux) and the parent metal. Slower than MIG but requires no gas supply, making it portable for site work.
Key Fact

Soft soldering < 450 °C, parent metal not melted. Brazing > 450 °C (brass filler rod), parent metal not melted. Welding: parent metal melts — this is what distinguishes it from all other thermal joining methods.

Soft soldering: temp < 450 °C | filler: tin alloy | parent metal: does NOT melt | materials: copper, steel, PCB | use: electronics, plumbing

Hard soldering / silver soldering: temp 450–900 °C | filler: silver alloy | parent metal: does NOT melt | materials: copper, brass | use: plumbing, jewellery

Brazing: temp ~870 °C | filler: brass rod | parent metal: does NOT melt | materials: steel, copper | use: pipework, bicycle frames, small engineering assemblies

Welding (MIG/arc): temp > 1500 °C | filler: electrode wire | parent metal: MELTS | materials: steel (MIG/arc), aluminium (MIG) | use: structures, vehicles, fabrication

knowledge_checks.q: What is the first stage of the riveting sequence that students most often omit?
At what approximate temperature does brazing occur, and does it melt the parent metal?
options: Below 450 °C; the parent metal does not melt
Around 870 °C; the parent metal does not melt

knowledge_checks.q: Welding is distinguished from brazing because in welding the _____ melts at the joint.
MIG welding shields the molten pool from oxygen using a flow of _____ gas such as argon or CO2.
Match each joining method to its key characteristic:
right: Tin alloy filler below 450 °C; parent metal not melted; used for PCBs and plumbing
Brass filler rod ~870 °C; parent metal not melted; used for steel and copper
Parent metal melts; produces a strong fusion bond for structural steel

before.content_html:
Why Heat-Treat Metals?

The mechanical properties of a metal — its hardness, strength, ductility and toughness — are determined not only by its chemical composition but also by the size and arrangement of the crystals (grains) inside it. Heat treatment deliberately alters grain structure by controlling how a metal is heated and then cooled. This gives engineers the ability to adjust properties after manufacturing: soften a steel so it can be bent without cracking, or harden a cutting tool so it keeps its edge under use.

All heat-treatment processes for carbon steel share three stages: heat to a soaking temperature appropriate for the process; hold at that temperature long enough for heat to penetrate the section (soaking); then cool at a controlled rate. The soaking temperature and cooling rate together determine which process you are performing and what properties result.

Normalising

Normalising restores a uniform grain structure after a manufacturing process that has distorted it. Forging, rolling, welding and cold working all introduce internal stresses and can produce a coarse or non-uniform grain. Normalising heats the steel above its upper critical temperature (typically 830–900 °C for medium-carbon steels) and then allows it to cool in still air. The still-air cooling rate is moderate — faster than furnace cooling, slower than water quenching — producing a fine, uniform grain structure. The result is a steel with improved toughness and consistent mechanical properties throughout the section.

Key Fact

Four key processes, four distinct purposes: Normalise = restore uniform grain after work-hardening or welding. Anneal = fully soften for further cold working. Harden + quench = maximise hardness (but brittle). Temper = reduce brittleness after hardening. These must not be confused with one another.

Annealing

Annealing is the process of making a metal as soft and ductile as possible. The steel is heated to above its upper critical temperature (same range as normalising) and then cooled very slowly — typically inside the furnace with the power switched off, taking many hours. This slow cooling gives atoms time to arrange themselves into large, coarse grains with very few dislocations, maximising ductility and making the metal easy to cold-work (bend, draw or stamp) without cracking.

Process annealing (also called sub-critical annealing or “softening”) is a variant used between stages of wire drawing or sheet rolling: the steel is heated just below the critical temperature and cooled slowly. This relieves the work-hardening that accumulates with each cold-working pass, allowing further deformation without fracture.

Hardening

Hardening makes carbon steel as hard as possible — but at the cost of making it brittle. The steel is heated above its upper critical temperature until it forms a uniform austenite structure throughout. It is then quenched (plunged rapidly into water, oil or brine). The sudden cooling prevents the atoms from reorganising into the soft structure they would normally form; instead, a highly stressed, needle-like microstructure called martensite is trapped. Martensite is extremely hard (the hardest microstructure in steel) but also very brittle — a hardened steel file will shatter rather than bend.

The choice of quench medium affects the cooling rate: water quenches fastest (maximum hardness, maximum distortion risk); oil is slower (slightly lower hardness, less distortion); brine (salt water) quenches fastest of all. For high-alloy steels, even air quenching may be fast enough to achieve full hardness.

A fully hardened steel is too brittle for most engineering applications — it would crack under impact. Tempering is always carried out after hardening to reduce brittleness while retaining as much hardness as possible. The hardened steel is reheated to a temperature below the lower critical temperature (typically 150–600 °C), held for a set time, then cooled in air. The heat allows some of the trapped martensite to transform to a tougher structure, releasing internal stresses.

The higher the tempering temperature, the tougher (and softer) the result. Colours appearing on a polished steel surface during tempering indicate the temperature reached: straw (230 °C) for woodworking chisels; blue (300 °C) for springs and screwdrivers; dark blue for saws. This temper colour method is a traditional way for a blacksmith to judge the tempering temperature without a thermometer.

Case Hardening

Case hardening is used when an engineer needs a component with a hard, wear-resistant surface and a tough, ductile core that resists impact. Gear teeth and camshaft lobes are classic examples: the surface must resist wear, but the core must resist the bending forces that would shatter a fully hardened component. Low-carbon steel (which normally cannot be hardened by quenching because it lacks sufficient carbon) is packed in a carbon-rich compound and heated in a furnace. Carbon diffuses into the outer layer over hours, raising the carbon content of the case to levels that allow hardening. The component is then quenched, hardening the carbon-enriched case while leaving the core (still low carbon) tough and ductile.

Key Fact

Case hardening gives a hard surface (to resist wear and pitting from contact forces) and a tough core (to resist the bending loads without shattering). Full through-hardening would make the gear tooth too brittle to withstand bending — it would snap rather than deform.

Normalising: heat above critical temp → cool in still air → result: uniform fine grain, relieved stresses, moderate improvement in toughness.

Annealing: heat above critical temp → cool very slowly in furnace → result: maximum ductility, coarse grain, softened for further cold working.

Hardening: heat above critical temp → quench rapidly in water/oil → result: maximum hardness (martensite) but brittle.

Tempering: reheat hardened steel below critical temp → cool in air → result: reduced brittleness, some hardness sacrificed for toughness.

Case hardening: heat low-carbon steel in carbon-rich atmosphere → carbon diffuses into surface layer → quench → result: hard case + tough core.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the annealing process?
A) Steel is heated above its critical temperature and cooled rapidly in water
B) Steel is heated above its critical temperature and cooled slowly inside the furnace
C) Steel is heated above its critical temperature and cooled in still air
D) Low-carbon steel is heated in a carbon-rich atmosphere and then quenched
practice_questions.marks: B) Steel is heated above its critical temperature and cooled slowly inside the furnace [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the purpose of tempering and explain why it is always carried out after hardening.
practice_questions.marks:
Tempering reduces the brittleness of hardened steel [1 mark].
Hardening produces a fully martensitic structure that is very hard but brittle and would crack under impact; tempering partially converts the martensite to a tougher structure so the component can withstand service loads without shattering [1 mark].
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a steel gear wheel used in a gearbox is case hardened rather than fully hardened throughout its section.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Explain Application of a Property or Material
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clearly explains both what case hardening achieves (hard surface + tough core) and why full through-hardening is unsuitable (would be too brittle, gear tooth would shatter under bending load), linking both to the specific service requirements of a gear wheel.

Secure (3-4 marks): Both surface hardness (wear resistance) and core toughness identified, with some explanation of the consequence of full hardening. May be underdeveloped on one point.

Developing (1-2 marks): One property mentioned with limited explanation; little link to the gear wheel application.

Content that may be credited:
- Gear teeth experience high contact stresses on their surface from meshing with other gears — the surface must be hard to resist wear and pitting.
- Gear teeth also experience bending loads at the root — the core must be tough to resist these without fracture.
- Full through-hardening would produce a uniform martensite structure throughout — extremely hard but brittle — the tooth would snap under bending rather than deform.
- Case hardening uses a low-carbon steel core (tough, ductile) with a high-carbon case diffused to a depth of typically 0.5–1.5 mm, then quenched to harden only the case.
- Result: surface has the hardness (typically 60–62 HRC) for wear resistance; the core retains toughness to carry the bending load.

practice_questions.text:
A low-carbon steel shaft has been cold-drawn to a reduced diameter. The manufacturing engineer wants to remove the internal stresses and restore ductility before further forming.

Identify the most appropriate heat treatment and describe the process stages.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Most appropriate heat treatment: Annealing [1 mark].
Process stages (award one mark each for any three):
- Heat the steel above its upper critical temperature (e.g. 830–880 °C for low-carbon steel) and soak until uniform temperature throughout
- Turn off the furnace and allow the steel to cool very slowly inside the furnace (do NOT remove and air-cool)
- The slow cooling produces a coarse, ductile grain structure with minimal internal stress
- The resulting steel is soft and ductile, suitable for further cold working
[4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the cooling rate after heating affects the resulting properties of a carbon steel. Refer to normalising and hardening in your answer.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Normalising: heated above critical temperature, cooled in still air (moderate cooling rate). Result: fine, uniform grain structure; moderate hardness and toughness; internal stresses relieved.
Hardening: heated above critical temperature, quenched rapidly in water or oil (very fast cooling rate). Result: martensitic structure; maximum hardness but brittle; high internal stresses.
Comparison: the faster the cooling rate, the harder (and more brittle) the result. Still-air cooling (normalising) gives a balanced microstructure; rapid quenching (hardening) locks in maximum hardness at the cost of ductility.
Consequence: a normalised steel is used for general engineering applications; a hardened-then-tempered steel is used for cutting tools, springs and bearings.
[6 marks — award for developed comparative points. At least two properties compared for each process. No marks for description in isolation.]

practice_questions.text: Kestrel Tool Works Ltd manufactures high-speed steel twist drills that must be hard enough to cut mild steel but must not shatter when loaded. Describe the heat treatment sequence the manufacturer should apply after initial machining.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Full hardening-and-tempering sequence described with reasons for each stage linked to the service requirements of a twist drill (must cut mild steel — needs hardness; must not shatter under drilling loads — needs toughness). Tempering temperature range discussed.

Secure (5-6 marks): Hardening and tempering described. Some link to drill requirements. Reasoning present but may miss tempering temperature detail.

Developing (3-4 marks): Hardening described; tempering mentioned but not developed. Limited link to service requirements.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Generic heat treatment points with no clear sequence or link to scenario.

Content that may be credited:
1. Hardening: heat the high-speed steel twist drill above its upper critical temperature; hold to soak uniformly; quench in oil (high-speed steel is oil-hardened) to produce a hard martensitic structure.
2. Reason: martensite gives the hardness needed to cut mild steel without the cutting edges wearing or deforming.
3. Tempering: reheat the hardened drill to 150–250 °C (straw colour on polished surface), hold, then cool in air.
4. Reason: a fully hardened drill would be too brittle — the flutes would snap under the torque of drilling. Tempering converts some martensite to a tougher structure, improving toughness without significantly reducing hardness.
5. Result: the finished drill has sufficient hardness to cut mild steel and sufficient toughness to withstand the drilling loads in service.

before.content_html:
Why Surface Finish Matters

A surface finish does two things simultaneously: it protects the base material from corrosion and it gives the product its appearance. Both matter commercially: a rusted chassis is structurally weakened, and an ugly surface finish damages a brand. Surface finishing is the last manufacturing stage before a product leaves the factory, so faults here affect every unit that ships. Understanding which finish suits which material, environment and cost envelope is a key engineering decision that examiners test every year.

Surface Preparation

Every surface finishing process begins with preparation. Paint, dip coatings and electroplating all bond poorly to a surface contaminated with grease, rust, mill scale or dust. Standard preparation steps are: degrease (solvent or alkali wash), abrade (grit-blast or sandpaper to provide a mechanical key), rinse and dry. Skipping preparation is the most common cause of coating failure in industry. A well-prepared surface can make a cheap paint finish outperform an expensive electroplated coating applied to a dirty surface.

Painting and Spray Painting

Painting applies a liquid coating to the surface that dries or cures to form a continuous protective film. Spray painting uses compressed air to atomise paint into a fine mist that settles evenly across the surface. It is used on vehicle bodywork, metal furniture, machinery guarding and architectural steelwork. Multiple thin coats are better than one thick coat, which sags and cures unevenly. High-volume industrial lines use electrostatic spray guns that charge the paint droplets so they are attracted to the earthed metal workpiece, reducing overspray waste.

Advantages of painting: wide colour choice; low cost for low-volume work; can be applied on-site to large structures (e.g. the Forth Road Bridge). Limitations: can chip or scratch to expose bare metal, allowing corrosion to undercut the surrounding paint (the most common failure mode); requires ventilation and personal protective equipment (PPE) due to solvent fumes.

Key Fact

Paint can chip or scratch to expose bare metal. Once bare metal is exposed, corrosion undercuts the surrounding coating from underneath, spreading the failure zone. Galvanising (zinc coating) sacrificially protects even when scratched because zinc is more electrochemically active than iron and corrodes preferentially.

Dip Coating

Dip coating (sometimes called plastisol dipping or powder dip coating) involves heating the cleaned metal component to around 200 °C and then dipping it into a fluidised bed of thermoplastic powder (typically PVC or polyethylene). The hot metal melts the powder particles that contact it, building up a thick, rubbery coating. The component is then cured in an oven. Dishwasher racks, tool handles, garden-chair frames and cycle-basket wire forms are typical applications: the thick thermoplastic coating gives grip, insulates electrically, resists knocks and provides complete waterproofing.

Advantages over spray paint: the coating is much thicker (typically 1–3 mm vs 50–150 μm for paint), more chemically resistant, and resistant to impact without chipping. Limitations: colour range is narrower than paint; the process requires heating the component, so large structures cannot be dip-coated easily; it is more expensive than painting per unit for large flat surfaces where thin coverage is acceptable.

Spray paint: solvent-based or water-based liquid; thin coat (50–150 μm); wide colour range; can chip; low cost; suitable for on-site and large structures.

Powder coating: thermosetting polymer powder applied by electrostatic gun and oven-cured; thin but very hard and scratch-resistant coat; good colour range; cannot be applied on-site; better than paint for chip resistance.

Dip coating: thermoplastic powder, component heated and dipped; very thick, tough, rubbery coat; limited colour range; good grip and electrical insulation; best for wire forms and handles.

For an extended-response evaluation question, linking the choice to specific properties (coating thickness, chip resistance, grip, cost) and a specific application always earns the most marks.

Electroplating

Electroplating uses electricity to deposit a thin, uniform layer of a metal onto the workpiece surface. The component to be plated is made the cathode (negative electrode) in an electrolytic cell; the plating metal (e.g. chromium, nickel, gold, copper, zinc) forms the anode (positive electrode). Current flows through the electrolyte solution, dissolving metal from the anode and depositing it on the cathode surface. Chromium plating on car bumpers and taps gives a mirror finish and excellent corrosion resistance. Gold plating on electrical contacts reduces contact resistance and prevents oxidation. Zinc electroplating (electrogalvanising) protects steel fasteners.

Advantages: very thin (1–50 μm), dimensionally precise coating that adds almost no thickness to machined surfaces; excellent surface finish and appearance; can deposit expensive metals (gold, platinum) very economically because the layer is so thin. Limitations: the plating bath and anodes must be managed carefully; wastewater from plating is chemically hazardous and requires specialist disposal; not suitable for complex internal cavities where current density is uneven.

Galvanising

Galvanising coats steel with a layer of zinc. The dominant method is hot-dip galvanising: clean, fluxed steel is submerged in a bath of molten zinc at approximately 450 °C. The zinc reacts with the steel to form a series of intermetallic alloy layers, bonded much more strongly than a paint film. Street furniture, motorway crash barriers, agricultural machinery and structural steelwork are galvanised as standard.

Galvanising has one property that paint lacks: sacrificial (cathodic) protection. Zinc is more electrochemically active than iron; if the zinc coating is scratched through to bare steel, the zinc around the scratch corrodes preferentially, protecting the exposed iron. The zinc “sacrifices itself” to protect the steel. Paint has no such mechanism — a scratch allows moisture to reach the steel and corrosion spreads under the coating.

Key Fact

Zinc is more electrochemically active than iron. When both are in contact with moisture, zinc corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection), so even a scratch through the galvanised coating does not allow the underlying steel to rust. Paint has no electrochemical activity — a chip exposes bare steel directly to moisture.

Polishing and Anodising

Polishing removes surface roughness mechanically — using abrasive compounds, buffing wheels or electropolishing — to produce a reflective, smooth surface. It is used on cutlery, surgical instruments, jewellery and any part where appearance or hygiene demands a smooth surface (rough surfaces trap bacteria). Polishing alone does not protect against corrosion but prepares the surface for electroplating or lacquering.

Anodising is specific to aluminium. Aluminium naturally forms a thin oxide layer that protects it from further corrosion, but anodising deliberately thickens this oxide layer using electrolysis. The anodised surface is hard, scratch-resistant and porous: dye can be absorbed into the pores before sealing, giving a wide range of colours. Laptop casings, window frames, bicycle components and camera bodies are commonly anodised. Unlike paint or plating, the anodised layer is part of the aluminium itself and cannot peel.

Ask three questions to choose the right finish: 1. What material is the workpiece? (Aluminium → anodising is most appropriate. Steel → galvanising, electroplating, paint or dip coating all possible.) 2. What environment will it face? (Outdoor, wet, salt spray → galvanising; food contact → electropolished stainless; decorative indoor → electroplating or paint.) 3. What is the production volume? (High volume → galvanising or electroplating bath; low volume or on-site → spray paint; small components needing grip → dip coating.)

For a 6- or 8-mark extended response comparing two surface finishes, the examiner rewards “similarities and key differences” rather than isolated bullet points about each finish. Always name the application, the mechanism of corrosion protection, the process steps and one limitation before concluding which is better for the specific scenario.

flashcard_questions.a: Chemical or electrochemical degradation — most commonly iron oxidising to rust in the presence of moisture and oxygen.
Grease, rust or scale prevents adhesion, causing the coating to fail prematurely.
flashcard_questions.q: Why must surface preparation be done before any coating is applied?

flashcard_questions.a: Applying paint as a fine mist under compressed air to produce a uniform, thin, even coat.
Giving wire forms and handles a thick, tough, rubbery thermoplastic coating for grip and waterproofing.
flashcard_questions.q: What is dip coating used for in engineering?

flashcard_questions.a: Immersing clean steel in a bath of molten zinc at about 450 °C to form a bonded zinc-iron alloy layer.
Zinc is more electrochemically active than iron and corrodes preferentially, protecting the steel even when scratched.
flashcard_questions.q: Why does galvanising provide sacrificial protection?

flashcard_questions.a: Cathode (negative electrode) — metal ions are deposited onto it from the anode.
flashcard_questions.q: In electroplating, what does the component being plated act as — anode or cathode?
Name one metal commonly deposited by electroplating on steel taps and car trim.

flashcard_questions.a: Electrochemically thickening the natural oxide layer; used on aluminium only.
flashcard_questions.q: What is anodising, and which metal is it used for?

flashcard_questions.a: The anodised layer is part of the aluminium itself and cannot peel or chip off.
flashcard_questions.q: Name one advantage of anodising over painting for an aluminium surface.

flashcard_questions.a: Polishing removes surface roughness for appearance and hygiene but does not form a protective barrier against moisture or oxygen.
flashcard_questions.q: Why is polishing alone insufficient as a corrosion-protection method?

flashcard_questions.a: Plating bath chemicals (heavy metals, acids) are hazardous and require specialist wastewater treatment and disposal.
flashcard_questions.q: Give one limitation of electroplating in terms of environmental impact.
